rationale: B wins by a nose because it is meaner about proof and timing, especially the line: "Without at least the time period, this angle is a bare number and should not be pitched." A has real usable lanes, especially "Patagonia won't say how big its resale business actually is," but it also lets "Patagonia expands a program built to sell you less clothing" skate too close to motive-as-fact. B still needs surgery on its ownership angle, but its refused angles and uncomfortable questions would save a founder from pitching half-baked copy.
gaps_in_A: "Patagonia expands a program built to sell you less clothing" overstates intent; the update gives repair economics and no apparel launch, not proof Patagonia is deliberately reducing new-unit sales.
"How to get Patagonia gear repaired for free" over-promises; only basic repairs are free and complex repairs are charged at cost.
"whether a national chain putting free repair drop-off in 70+ stores plus mail-in is evidence the category itself has matured" needs outside market proof before it becomes a trend story.
Next step jumps to `find-journalists`; it should first test whether Worn Wear has already been covered to death and what is materially new.
gaps_in_B: "A company with no shareholders" is not in the supplied facts; private ownership is not the same as no shareholders.
"nobody else can copy the math" is a big, unsupported competitive claim. It needs cost data and peer evidence before it goes anywhere near a reporter.
"category-creation" is a flabby label for what is really a retail-ops/reverse-logistics story.

It throws away the consumer service lane too fast with "Patagonia customers can now mail in their gear for free repairs" as a duplicate; a clean how-it-works piece could still land if the free-versus-paid boundary is nailed down.
